title: Medicare Will Now Cover Ozempic and Wegovy for Weight Loss — Here's Who Qualifies and What It Costs
excerpt: A new pilot program launching July 1 lets eligible seniors get GLP-1 drugs for just $50 a month, but the fine print matters — and the clock is already ticking.
body:
The most significant shift in obesity treatment coverage for American seniors in decades goes live today. Starting July 1, Medicare will cover GLP-1 weight-loss medications — including Novo Nordisk's Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Zepbound — for the first time, through a temporary pilot program called the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge.

Under the program, eligible Medicare Part D enrollees can access these drugs for a flat $50 monthly copay, regardless of the medication's list price. Without coverage, these drugs can cost anywhere from $149 to over $1,000 per month depending on the specific drug, dosage, and whether it's a pill or injection.

## What Changed — and Why It Matters

Federal law has long prohibited Medicare from covering drugs prescribed solely for weight loss. The GLP-1 Bridge sidesteps that restriction through a demonstration program created by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services under Dr. Mehmet Oz. It was formulated as part of the Trump administration's "most favored nations" drug pricing framework, which ties US prices to the lowest rates paid by comparable developed countries.

The program covers Wegovy tablets and injections, Zepbound KwikPens, and Foundayo tablets — the three branded formulations that have reshaped obesity medicine over the past three years. Medicare Part D already covers GLP-1 drugs for Type 2 diabetes, heart disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and fatty liver disease, but this is the first time obesity alone qualifies.

## Who Qualifies

Not every Medicare enrollee is eligible. Patients must be enrolled in Medicare Part D and meet specific BMI and health criteria:

- **BMI above 35**: Eligible directly.
- **BMI between 30 and 35**: Must also have one of several qualifying conditions — uncontrolled high blood pressure, prediabetes, a previous heart attack or stroke, blocked arteries with symptoms, or chronic kidney disease at Stage 3a or higher.
- **BMI between 27 and 30**: Must have prediabetes, a prior heart attack or stroke, or symptomatic blocked arteries.

Critically, patients already receiving GLP-1 drugs through their Medicare plan for other conditions — diabetes, sleep apnea, or fatty liver — are excluded from the Bridge. New estimates from KFF, a health policy research group, suggest approximately 3.8 million Medicare beneficiaries would have met the program's specific criteria, a meaningful but narrower pool than the 13.3 million who meet BMI thresholds for obesity or being overweight.

## The Fine Print

Doctors must certify that patients are using the medication alongside a structured lifestyle program incorporating diet and exercise. Prior authorization is required, and the approval process could slow initial uptake as patients and providers navigate the system.

The $50 copay does not count toward a patient's annual deductible or out-of-pocket maximum — a notable departure from standard Part D cost-sharing rules. Once approved, coverage runs through December 31, 2027.

That expiration date is the program's most consequential caveat. GLP-1 drugs are long-term maintenance medications. Research consistently shows that patients who discontinue them regain lost weight, and the rebound tends to be disproportionately fat rather than muscle. "Not only will weight come back, comorbidities will come back," warned Dr. John Batsis, a geriatrician and obesity specialist at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine. "When you gain it back, you're gaining more fat than muscle."

## The Diaspora Dimension

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian Americans in the United States — many of whom are managing multigenerational households — the program carries particular weight. South Asians face elevated metabolic risk at lower BMI thresholds than the general population: the WHO recommends that South Asians be screened for diabetes at a BMI of 23, not 25, reflecting higher rates of visceral fat and insulin resistance.

Many NRI families are navigating Medicare coverage for aging parents while simultaneously managing their own employer-sponsored insurance. With several major employers cutting GLP-1 coverage for working-age adults this year — a Mercer survey found 6% of large employers dropped coverage in 2026 and another 5% plan to in 2027 — the generational divide in access is sharpening.

The Bridge program offers a window, but it's a narrow one. NRI families with eligible relatives should discuss the program with their physicians now, given that prior authorization can take time and demand for the medications has persistently outstripped supply.

**Sources:** Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS); KFF Medicare policy analysis (June 2026); MarketWatch; USA Today; Mercer employer survey (June 2026).
